.@sophiadew says radiology is proof AI can transform jobs instead of eliminating them. @AndrewYang says the transition is happening far too fast for that story to hold:

Sophia: "I am an optimist because of all of your fears that you say. There are certain things that we should do to mitigate all the harms that AI will cause."

"Most people think one day robots are going to come in and all the jobs are going to leave, but what actually ends up happening is a slow transition where the jobs transform and re-augment in ways where the human has to do more human type of work."

"Everyone thought AI would get rid of all the radiologists. There's more demand for radiology, but the job of a radiologist now is way more human."

Andrew Yang: "I'm now 50 years old, which means if I don't get dumber in a given month, it was a good month. Meanwhile, the models will get twice as smart that month."

"Block fired 4,000 out of 10,000. Oracle laid off 30,000 workers and said, we're doing it to invest in AI. This is not a multi-year transition. This is like a hey, sorry, we don't need you anymore."
@jubileemedia

I'm definitely not "fighting the Church thesis." 

But, as @wtgowers pointed out, there is a questio...
items.content:
I'm definitely not "fighting the Church thesis." 

But, as @wtgowers pointed out, there is a question of practicality and efficiency. 

The real world is highly complex, messy, and not entirely predictable.
It is *somewhat* predictable *IF* you accept the fact that you need to find an appropriate representation of the state of the world that allows you to make predictions by ignore much of the information about the state of the system that is simply not predictable in practice (what physicists have called entropy).

For example, I can predict that the pressure in a box full of air will increase if I heat it up. This is because of the law of ideal gas pV=nRT.
But there is absolutely no way in hell I can simulate the individual positions and velocities of every molecule of air in the box. Even though this is the underlying physical phenomenon with known laws, it's totally useless at a macroscopic scale, particularly for a system in interaction with the rest of the universe.

So, the Church thesis, while true, is irrelevant to this discussion.
items.author: @ylecun
items.summary: Continuing our coverage from [yesterday](/?date=2026-09-27&category=social#item-2bcca08e90dc), Yann LeCun pushes back on the claim he is fighting the Church thesis, arguing the real issue is practicality and efficiency: the world is only partially predictable, and useful prediction requires finding compressed representations that discard unpredictable details, illustrated with the ideal gas law versus molecular simulation.
items.reasoning: High author credibility (LeCun, a leading AI researcher) and genuine technical/philosophical depth on world models and prediction, but very low engagement (5 likes, 858 views) and it is a fragment of a longer debate rather than breaking news.

.@schisofrenia argues the real UBI question is how AI wealth gets redistributed. @AndrewYang says he’s already seen one version of it firsthand after getting paid $2,500 for AI to use his work:

Sofia: "You were the person who first introduced me to the concept of UBI in the first place"

"We have a sovereign wealth fund, akin to what Norway has. Alaska has more of a petroleum dividend."

"You could do things like wage insurance. If somebody made 80k a year and their job was displaced by AI and they have to get a job that's 50k a year, the government could compensate those people for the amount that they lost."

Andrew Yang: "I am probably the only person in this circle who actually did get paid for their data. AI wants to eat your book and it will pay you $2,500 for the privilege. Imagine if every American got a message like that."
@jubileemedia

Being in the AI business is brutal when your customers figure out there are cheaper ways to do it.

...
items.content:
Being in the AI business is brutal when your customers figure out there are cheaper ways to do it.

@NinjaTechAI showed me last week exactly this.

Long-running agents in enterprise: all running on machines under control of the company. “On prem” everyone calls it.

“Take no dependencies,” the rallying cry says.

Ninja announces within days but already has big companies lining up and it hasn’t even released. 

Word of mouth spreads fast because CTOs have their jobs on the line if they don’t pick the right architecture/vendors/technology.

Running local open source models is attracting customers in enterprise.

Turns out enterprise usually doesn’t need the best of the best models either.

Enterprises need consistency more than ultimate intelligence. 

There are a lot more Ian’s out there.

So big shifts still ahead as the world’s business learns to use AI to make bottom lines better.

Right now many are dumping cash into tokens and not getting enough ROI out of the spend. I hear this from many.

items.title:
Multiple things can be true at the same time:

1. Closed, frontier models are generally smarter than...
items.content:
Multiple things can be true at the same time:

1. Closed, frontier models are generally smarter than local models[*].

2. Local models are extremely capable and more than enough for many applications.

3. You can fine-tune open models and run them very fast, for very little money, and outperform even the best frontier models from Big AI labs on many problems.

(*) I've seen people interpret the term "local" in different ways. In this context, I assume "local" refers to open models you can host yourself.
items.author: @svpino
items.summary: @svpino argues that several seemingly conflicting views about model choice are simultaneously true: closed frontier models are generally smarter, local open models are already capable enough for many applications, and fine-tuned open models can run cheaply and fast while beating frontier models on specific problems. He also clarifies his definition of local as self-hosted open models.
items.reasoning: A nuanced, original take on the open vs. closed model debate from a recognizable ML practitioner with solid engagement (93 likes, ~15k views). The balanced framing is useful for practitioners deciding between hosted frontier APIs and fine-tuned self-hosted models, though it lacks technical depth or new evidence.

items.title: Single class classifiers (machine learning one-class classification OCC algorithms) are often overlo...
items.content:
Single class classifiers (machine learning one-class classification OCC algorithms) are often overlooked when dealing with multi-class datasets.

Why would OCC be considered useful? Well, if you try to maximize performance across a multidimensional objective function, you tend to allow larger errors in some classes in order to reduce error in other (perhaps difficult-to-classify) classes. Sacrificing performance in perhaps one of the most critical classes simply to make the overall model look good can be a poor decision. RMSE is an example of a metric that minimizes error over a large range of data, which could be dangerous when the accuracy of one smaller segment of the data really requires higher performance than the rest of the data. 

Example: looking for fraud (a specific category of behavior) in a complex financial data ecosystem (representing many different “normal” behaviors) should receive specific targeted attention. Who cares if you classify with high accuracy all the non-fraud categories during your first machine learning classification run over the dataset. First separate fraud from non-fraud cases with the highest possible accuracy. Then deal urgently with these fraud cases, as highest priority. Then, the non-fraud group of numerous diverse behavior categories can be partitioned with your favorite multi-class classifier(s) according to the organization’s needs and requirements. Years ago, I did some consulting for a large federal agency where we did exactly this!

Similar examples can be given in other domains: acute medical diagnoses, network intrusions, industrial machine predictive maintenance monitoring, environmental monitoring, etc.

See the attached screenshot of Google’s AI response to my query about OCC.

So, the OCC can give you a gold standard classifier to serve your highest priority need first. Then you can resume normal machine learning. 😎

More about OCC: https://t.co/drBkTmLuMy

ML Mastery tutorial: https://t.co/dCraiG5CZc

Review of techniques [35-page PDF]: https://t.co/ltvLKZlhmR

Build a Reasoning Model (From Scratch): https://t.co/IzY3D4m8nG by @rasbt via @ManningBooks 
🌟🌟🌟🌟🌟
Amazon summary:

The book is especially useful because it implements the core methods from scratch rather than treating them as black-box library calls. Readers see how self-consistency, self-refinement, Best-of-N, and training-based methods actually work, including their cost and latency trade-offs. 

The book also discusses common failure modes, including cases where refinement can make answers worse. Difficult concepts such as softmax, temperature, and top-p sampling are clarified with code-linked explanations and diagrams, while visual workflows make pipelines and scoring methods easier to follow.

Reading the book feels like following a guided technical build rather than a loose survey of AI topics. Each concept is introduced because the project now needs it. Diagrams, roadmaps, code listings, exercises, and repeated workflow summaries help readers stay oriented through advanced material.

items.title:
My thoughts on the quoted post down below…

I think that an interesting (and potentially illuminatin...
items.content:
My thoughts on the quoted post down below…

I think that an interesting (and potentially illuminating) experiment would be to put a large number of these AI-powered hedge fund trading agents in a closed sandbox (simulated market) and watch what happens. Does one agent ultimately become lord over all agents? Do they all win? Or do they all lose? Or does it converge on a state with no winners or losers? Or do they actively act against (sabotage) one another? Or (worse case scenario) do they break out of the sandbox (as in some other recent experiments) and attack the real markets?

Genetic Algorithm (GA) simulations, anyone?

items.title: My first encounter with classic AI was nearly 40 years ago while working with NASA colleagues using ...
items.content: My first encounter with classic AI was nearly 40 years ago while working with NASA colleagues using LISP in a decision support software package for the Hubble Space Telescope. The rule-based syntax of LISP was very interesting and efficient, radically different from my years of mathematical scientific programming in FORTRAN, but LISP was ultimately abandoned since it required time-intensive development as new and more complex edge cases for the operational telescope systems regularly emerged. A highly successful O.R. decision support & scheduling system was eventually implemented, which NASA then open-sourced and spun off to other completely different industries. Nevertheless, my first encounter with “early AI” owes a lot to this guy… ⤵️

items.content:
Back in the 2000s my brother in law worked high up at Apple.

One day he told me Apple was working on the phone.

A few months later he told me Jobs killed the project.

A few months later he told me they were working on it again.

I would expect no less than a complete rethink every once in a while.

Consumers are changing which makes new things possible to sell.

I hope they kill all glasses.

And go with something Bono would wear on stage.

This reminds me of my boss’s words in the consumer electronics store: “sell what you got.”

The Snap @specs are the better view of the future.

Too bad it can’t do the Formula 1 experience.

Spent the budget on technology.

None left for the content.

Apple has pretty good content.

Apple could kill its glasses and license its content at a much higher profit.

But Apple hates how its content looks on other screens.

So I expect at the end of the day Apple will figure out how to put screens on our eyes.

And if not? ByteDance has a pair in the labs. TikTok trained AI. Light like the new Meta.

Which one do you think will have better content?

The new Apple CEO knows spatial computing better than pretty much anyone alive.

items.content:
.@AndrewYang says AI will crush millions of jobs. @theojaffee argues jobs don’t work that way and 200 years of automation says otherwise:

Andrew Yang: "2.9 million Americans work in customer service call centers. 2 million drive an Uber. 70 million Americans work at white collar jobs. I think AI is going to crush this number."

Theo: "Just looking at the past 200 years or so of automation, this claim has been made over and over again and it doesn't stand because automating jobs is really hard."

"Jobs are bundles of tasks. In order to automate a job, you have to do every single task the human does on some Pareto curve of better and cheaper than the human. If there's one task in a job remaining for humans to do, humans are still employable"

Andrew Yang: "There are 100 people in a department doing a job and if you can reduce 60% of the tasks, what happens is you fire 60 of the hundred and the remaining 40 you say, hey guys, your jobs just changed. Then you systematically reduce that number."
@jubileemedia

items.content: If *I* were to walk back into the classroom tomorrow, and go back to my Physics teaching days, I probably wouldn't change much, if anything. We are homeschooling our kids, and we are using primarily very traditional pencil-and-paper methods. I believe that doing a full-scale reform of education *right now* is like trying to catch a falling knife. It's best to wait and see how the whole AI transition will play out, and then rebuild all of our human institutions from ground up.

Sophia: "With Jevons paradox, as AI increases productivity, there also increases more demand. One of the biggest areas where we're seeing rise in demand are things that are uniquely human and that AI cannot replace."

Andrew Yang: "Graphic design used to be considered a creative task and now that's getting pounded out by AI. Video making, no offense Jubilee, that's getting mulched by AI."

"If I'm rich and I want someone to tell me what painting I should hang in my living room, I will pay a human to do it. That's only because the ultra winners are going to want people's taste."
@jubileemedia

items.title: Red-Bull:  @redbull From SAP BW on HANA to Jupyter + MLflow: SAP HANA Evolution! #SAPHANA with #Jupy...
items.content:
Red-Bull:  @redbull From SAP BW on HANA to Jupyter + MLflow: SAP HANA Evolution! #SAPHANA with #Jupyter Notebooks and MLFlow! 

Back in the day, I wrote about how SAP NetWeaver BW powered by SAP HANA was improving enterprise performance across industries such as beverages, utilities, and automotive and machine learning. 

Following algorithms available at the time: 
Classification: Decision Trees, Logistic Regression, Naïve BayesSAP Community Clustering: K-Means, DBSCAN, Hierarchical Clustering

Regression: Multiple Linear, Exponential, Polynomial
Time Series Forecasting: ARIMA, Exponential Smoothing
Association Rules: Apriori algorithms
Native R Integration (Rserve)
Automated Predictive Library (APL)
SAP Predictive Analysis Tool

Red-Bull was the early adopters of machine learning, moving its existing SAP NetWeaver BW landscape onto the SAP HANA in-memory database.
At the time, the implementation was primarily about speed, compression, rapid migration, and business continuity. Roughly 1.5 TB database and a rapid migration completed within about two weeks and project in about three years.

Fast-forward, and the performance has expanded into machine learning and data science. SAP HANA Cloud now supports in-database machine-learning capabilities through PAL/APL, while Python-based tooling lets data scientists work from environments such as Jupyter Notebooks without necessarily moving large datasets out of HANA for model execution. SAP also documents Python ML clients, classification, regression, forecasting, anomaly detection, and AutoML scenarios around HANA Cloud.

Szymon Godziek landed the first ever Tsunami Flip on a mountain bike in contest at the best trick showdown at Red Bull District Ride in that year!

items.title: I'm personally fine with high skilled vetted people with cultures that align with European culture t...
items.content:
I'm personally fine with high skilled vetted people with cultures that align with European culture to migrate to Europe, that's how migration to US or Australia or Korea works

But that should be just a certain % minority of society

It can't get close to replacing it

Just like having Europeans colonizing Africa was very wrong, having mass migration from Africa (and Middle East) into Europe is wrong and not a good idea

If you don't believe me check the famously shared Danish crime numbers per origin showing extreme overrepresentation of MENA countries

I also keep seeing this mentioned as if now it's "payback time" for the Europeans which is a fallacious take

You're taking DHH's point personal when it's not personal, you're welcome if you're high skilled and contribute, he'd probably say the same

That doesn't mean we have to just accept anyone coming into Europe without vetting like the open borders we had for the last decades, because that's negatively affecting our societies now

items.content:
Anatomy of a 20 Sec Earthquake! #BigData #Analytics #AI #MachineLearning #DataScience #IoT #IIoT #Python #RStats #TensorFlow #JavaScript #ReactJS #CloudComputing #Serverless #GeoSpatial #DataScientist #Linux #Programming #Coding #100DaysofCode  

I was right in the middle of Hermosa Beach earthquake! I started my morning warm up at about 830 am and walk from Redondo Beach at 8:55 AM, walking to the 24 Hour Fitness in Hermosa Beach and back, covering 2.77 miles in 1:05:06. I’ll be going back to the same 24 Hour Fitness in a few hours for my workout!
Just 15 minutes before I started walking, at approximately 8:40 AM, a magnitude 3.5 earthquake struck offshore, about 3.7 miles west-southwest of Hermosa Beach at a depth of roughly 7 miles. Early reports listed the earthquake at magnitude 3.5, with subsequent reporting indicating that the U.S. Geological Survey revised it to magnitude 3.6.

Some reports described approximately 20 seconds of earthquake. No injuries or significant damage were immediately reported. 

References 

ABC7 Los Angeles. (2026, September 27). 3.6-magnitude earthquake strikes Hermosa Beach area, USGS says. Retrieved from https://t.co/rNikCf3T4y
Turner, A. (2026, September 27). Preliminary 3.5-magnitude earthquake strikes near Hermosa Beach. CBS News Los Angeles. Retrieved from https://t.co/O6eYN97ATA
U.S. Geological Survey. (2026). Earthquake Hazards Program. Retrieved September 27, 2026, from https://t.co/PPVCppnqWb

Anatomy of a 20 Sec Earthquake! #BigData #Analytics #AI #MachineLearning #DataScience #IoT #IIoT #Python #RStats #TensorFlow #JavaScript #ReactJS #CloudComputing #Serverless #GeoSpatial #DataScientist #Linux #Programming #Coding #100DaysofCode

I was right in the middle of Hermosa Beach earthquake! I started my morning warm up at about 830 am and walk from Redondo Beach at 8:55 AM, walking to the 24 Hour Fitness in Hermosa Beach and back, covering 2.77 miles in 1:05:06. I’ll be going back to the same 24 Hour Fitness in a few hours for my workout!

Just 15 minutes before I started walking, at approximately 8:40 AM, a magnitude 3.5 earthquake struck offshore, about 3.7 miles west-southwest of Hermosa Beach at a depth of roughly 7 miles. Early reports listed the earthquake at magnitude 3.5, with subsequent reporting indicating that the U.S. Geological Survey revised it to magnitude 3.6.

Some reports described approximately 20 seconds of earthquake. No injuries or significant damage were immediately reported.

References

items.content:
It’s a complex issue as much of your hypothesis is a theory undone by the rich simply leaving the UK which now has the lowest levels of millionaires since 2008.

My suggestion is give tax exemptions where if the wealthy invest into a government approved venture or project that creates skilled employment and growth they are tax exempt of that amount - a scaled up SEIS and EIS. Then loopholes are not needed.

items.title: You don’t live in England and clearly have missed all the comments critical of Maguire, Shaw, Connor...
items.content:
You don’t live in England and clearly have missed all the comments critical of Maguire, Shaw, Connor Gallagher, Foden, and even Harry Kane gets criticised. In the past so too was Gerrard, Rooney and Lampard. 
True there is some racism here but it’s far better than Spain, Italy, a number of the Arabic teams  and many other national football teams. 

English football has a long history of always blaming the team due to over expectations and simply not willing to accept that Spain or another given team might just be better than England. So perpetually the players have failed since 1966.
